passage: Thanks for asking, Rajni. When I moved to Manchester, my flatmate Owen kept looking puzzled when I answered questions with a head wobble. I hadn't noticed I was doing it. I explained, laughing, that it means something like okay or I hear you, and Owen said, "So, yes?" We settled on me saying yes out loud as well. Then there was me on the phone to my mother in the shared kitchen, loud as at home; Owen was polite until I noticed his face, and I took the call to my room. I also learnt not to ask a new colleague about salary in the first week, which I thought was friendly. Not everyone from home does these things, but I did, and a bit of explaining and adapting helped us both enjoy it. Pradeep

qa.q: Where did Pradeep move to?
qa.a: Pradeep moved to Manchester.

qa.q: What did Pradeep feel on noticing Owen's face during the phone call?
qa.a: Self-conscious but considerate; seeing the face made Pradeep take the call to the bedroom.

qa.q: What did Pradeep and Owen do about the head wobble?
qa.a: They settled on Pradeep saying yes out loud as well.

qa.q: How might Owen have felt about the head wobble at first?
qa.a: Puzzled, unsure whether it meant yes or no, which is why Owen asked, So, yes?

grounding: A young Indian abroad notices that head-wobbling, a salary question and a loud call may surprise hosts, and explains kindly and adapts.

subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
passage: I'm Madhuri, and I work two desks from Gurpreet at a software firm in Toronto. In Gurpreet's first week I watched a small scene. Gurpreet asked a new teammate, cheerfully, "So how much do you earn, and are you married?" The teammate blinked, laughed politely and changed the subject. Later, in the lounge, Gurpreet took a call from home and spoke loudly; two people looked up. I can't know how Gurpreet felt about those glances. That afternoon I told Gurpreet quietly that back home those questions show interest, but here many people save them for close friends. Gurpreet nodded slowly and said, "Oh, I see." The next day Gurpreet asked the teammate about the weekend instead, and calls moved to the corridor.

qa.q: Where does Madhuri work?
qa.a: Madhuri works at a software firm in Toronto.

qa.q: Why did Madhuri speak to Gurpreet quietly that afternoon?
qa.a: To explain kindly without embarrassing Gurpreet, since the questions came from interest, not rudeness.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet change afterwards?
qa.a: Gurpreet asked the teammate about the weekend instead, and moved calls to the corridor.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet have felt about the glances in the lounge?
qa.a: Possibly puzzled or a little self-conscious, though Madhuri cannot know for sure.

grounding: A young Indian abroad sees a colleague's personal questions and loud call surprise hosts and explains kindly, and the colleague adapts.

passage:
Monday: In the Dublin flat, Varun's roommate Ramesh answered his mother's call on speaker at seven in the morning, shouting cheerfully in Telugu. Varun saw their Irish flatmate, Aoife, freeze in the kitchen doorway, eyebrows up.
Wednesday: At work, Varun heard Ramesh ask a new colleague, "How much do they pay you? Married?" The colleague laughed awkwardly and changed the subject. Varun noticed his own head wobbling "yes" in a meeting, and the manager said, "Is that a yes or a no?"
Saturday: Over pizza, Varun told Aoife and Ramesh, "Back home these things are normal. Salary questions are just curiosity. Loud calls mean we're close." Aoife laughed with relief. "I thought something was wrong!" Ramesh agreed to take early calls on the balcony. Varun started adding a clear "yes". Aoife asked if she could learn the wobble.

qa.q: What did Ramesh ask the new colleague?
qa.a: "How much do they pay you? Married?"

qa.q: What was Varun feeling as he noticed Aoife freeze in the doorway?
qa.a: Varun felt surprised and a little embarrassed, seeing that a normal morning call from home startled their flatmate.

qa.q: Which steps helped the flat, and why?
qa.a: Varun explained kindly what the habits meant, and both adapted a little, with calls on the balcony and a clear yes, so neither side felt judged.

qa.q: How did Aoife see the loud calls before Varun explained?
qa.a: Aoife seemed worried that something was wrong, and was relieved to learn they were just a close family's normal chat.

grounding: It illustrates a young Indian abroad who notices Indian habits surprising hosts and helps both sides with a kind explanation and small adjustments.

subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
passage: Rashmi, you're going to Toronto soon, so listen to your Nikita masi. When I was twenty-five, on my first job there, I sat at lunch with a nice colleague named Sarah and asked her, as naturally as asking the time, "How much salary are you getting? And why aren't you married yet?" She went red. The whole table went quiet. I didn't understand. My mother asked her friends those things every day! That evening I nearly cried. I felt like a village girl in the big city. But the next day I told Sarah, "Sorry, at home those are friendly questions. I didn't mean to pry." She laughed and said her own grandmother asks the same. We became real friends after that. She even learnt to say "chalo" when leaving. So be yourself, beta, but watch faces.

qa.q: What did young Nikita ask Sarah at lunch?
qa.a: "How much salary are you getting? And why aren't you married yet?"

qa.q: How did young Nikita feel that evening?
qa.a: She felt confused and ashamed, nearly crying and feeling out of place in the big city.

qa.q: What was the key choice in Nikita's story, and why did it work?
qa.a: Explaining kindly to Sarah the next day that the questions were friendly at home; it cleared the awkwardness and opened a real friendship.

qa.q: How might Sarah have felt when asked about her salary and marriage?
qa.a: Sarah was probably embarrassed and caught off guard, since those are private topics for her, and then relieved by the kind explanation.

grounding: It illustrates a young Indian abroad who notices that questions about salary and marriage surprise hosts, and explains kindly and adapts.

subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
passage:
The regional train from Munich to Nuremberg was already forty minutes late, and Zubin and his colleague Hrithik had squeezed into the only two free seats, in the quiet carriage. Hrithik's phone rang. It was his mother, and he answered on speaker, loudly: "Haan Mummy, haan, khaana kha liya!" Zubin saw a woman opposite lower her book and stare. A man across the aisle pointed at the little sign showing a crossed-out phone.
Zubin's cheeks went warm. He leaned over. "Hrithik, quiet coach. Take it in the corridor?" Hrithik looked startled, then grinned and went. Zubin turned to the woman. "Sorry, his mother calls every day. It's a kind of love, just loud." She smiled, and so did the man. When Hrithik came back, he whispered, "Why didn't anyone tell me?" The train crawled on. Zubin sent him a photo of the sign.

qa.q: What did the little sign across the aisle show?
qa.a: A crossed-out phone.

qa.q: What was Zubin feeling when the woman lowered her book and stared?
qa.a: Zubin felt embarrassed, his cheeks going warm, aware that Hrithik's loud call was bothering the passengers.

qa.q: Which of Zubin's two moves helped, and why?
qa.a: Quietly asking Hrithik to take the call to the corridor, and kindly explaining to the woman that it was a caring mother; this eased both sides without shaming anyone.

qa.q: How might Hrithik have seen the moment?
qa.a: Hrithik seemed surprised and a little sheepish, not having known about the quiet coach, and grateful someone told him kindly.

grounding: It illustrates a young Indian abroad noticing that a loud phone call surprises locals, and explaining kindly while adapting a little.

subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
passage: Sabina's Sunday call to Lucknow could be heard from the stairwell. "Haan Ammi, I ate! No, not married yet, stop!" In the kitchen of their Melbourne flat, Chloe paused with the kettle, eyebrows up. Avni noticed. Last night Sabina had asked Chloe how much her new job paid and whether her boyfriend planned to propose, and Chloe had laughed too brightly and changed the subject. Later Sabina had wobbled her head at Chloe's question about dinner, and Chloe had waited, unsure if that meant yes. After the call, Avni made three cups of tea. "Chloe, where we grew up, lots of people ask about pay and marriage to show they care. And that head wobble usually means yes." Chloe grinned. "Good to know. I thought I'd offended her." Later Avni told Sabina gently, "Here those questions feel private. Maybe take Ammi's calls on the balcony?" Sabina rolled her eyes, then carried her phone outside.

qa.q: What did Sabina ask Chloe the night before?
qa.a: Sabina asked Chloe how much her new job paid and whether her boyfriend planned to propose.

qa.q: What might Avni have been worried about as she watched Chloe in the kitchen?
qa.a: Avni was uneasy that Chloe felt awkward and intruded on, and that her two flatmates were quietly misreading each other.

qa.q: How did Avni help both flatmates, and what made it work?
qa.a: She explained Sabina's habits kindly to Chloe and quietly suggested one small change to Sabina, so nobody felt blamed and both could adjust a little.

qa.q: How might Sabina feel about being asked to take calls on the balcony?
qa.a: Sabina may feel a bit annoyed or self-conscious, as the eye-roll shows, yet still goes outside, showing a willingness to adapt.

grounding: Shows a young Indian abroad noticing how personal questions, a head wobble and loud calls surprise a host, then explaining kindly so both sides adapt.
